resources.string: Anegada acacia
Vachellia anegadensis
thorny acacia
A very thorny small tree of the Virgin Islands. Fine bipinnate leaves, yellow pompom heads and curved pods distinguish it from phyllode-bearing acacias; the species is threatened and localized.
Endemic to the British Virgin Islands, especially Anegada and Virgin Gorda; coastal dry scrub.
Spreading shrub or small tree, often under 6 m, with strongly armed branches and long stipular spines.
Alternate bipinnate leaves divided into numerous tiny leaflets.
Small spherical yellow flower heads, grouped in the leaf axils.
Curved brown pod that opens at maturity and contains several seeds.
Mathuata acacia
Acacia mathuataensis
Fijian Mathuata acacia
A spreading Fijian acacia or small tree. Its type specimen records spreading habit and vivid yellow petals and stamens; pod characters are poorly documented, so the plate keeps that detail generic.
Fiji, recorded from the Mathuata district of Vanua Levu; tropical woodland.
Spreading small tree reaching about 6 m; crown form varies.
Alternate flattened, narrow phyllodes, typical of this acacia group; dimensions vary.
Globose heads with vivid yellow petals and stamens.
Legume pod; shape and details are poorly documented in the sources consulted.
Long-tubed Ambrella
Ambrella longituba
Ambrella orchid
A miniature epiphytic orchid of humid evergreen forests in northern Madagascar, with a long tubular labellum. It typically bears five or six leaves and an inflorescence with one to three flowers.
Northern Madagascar; epiphytic in humid evergreen forests.
Tiny epiphytic orchid forming a tuft of a few leaves; inflorescence with one to three flowers.
About five or six flat elliptic leaves gathered in a tuft.
Greenish flower with a tubular labellum up to about 4.5 cm, hairy inside.
Elongated capsule after pollination; rarely shown in available illustrations.
Thollon\'s Dioncophyllum
Dioncophyllum thollonii
Dioncophyllum liana
A large tropical liana with alternate simple leaves, some ending in hooks that help it climb. Unlike its close relative Triphyophyllum, it is not carnivorous.
Humid tropical forests of Gabon and the Congo Basin.
Woody climbing liana that can reach the canopy using hooked leaf tips.
Alternate simple leaves with marked longitudinal veins; some tips become hooks.
Small white flowers with five petals in inflorescences.
Dry capsule opening in several valves; seeds have membranous wings.
Glaucous halothamnus
Halothamnus glaucus
blue-green halothamnus
A gray-green subshrub of steppes and deserts in western Asia. Its fleshy leaves with pungent tips and papery winged fruit help distinguish it from related saltbushes.
Eastern Europe to Central Asia; steppes, semideserts and arid slopes.
Branched subshrub, usually 30–70 cm tall, with glabrous gray-green branches.
Alternate semiterete, fleshy linear leaves with pungent tips.
Minute flowers in loose spikes with membranous bracts.
Dry fruit with five yellow-brown wings forming a circular disk.
Corymb rose
Rosa cymosa
Chinese scrambling rose

An East Asian rose with long arching stems, leaves of three to seven toothed leaflets and clusters of small cream flowers. Its globose hips, sometimes dark red to nearly black, contrast with elongated hips such as those of Rosa pendulina.
Southern and eastern China to Vietnam; forest margins and thickets.
Scrambling shrub 2–5 m tall with long arching stems.
Compound leaf with three to seven elliptic or lanceolate, finely toothed leaflets.
Many cream-white flowers in compound corymbs with numerous stamens.
Small globose hip, red then sometimes deep purple or nearly black.
Showy Nectouxia
Nectouxia formosa
Chisos Nectouxia
A rhizomatous perennial of mountains in northern Mexico and Texas. Alternate glandular leaves, tubular corolla and narrow berries with many seeds characterize this rare nightshade.
Chisos Mountains and Big Bend in Texas and northern Mexico; rocky slopes around 2,100–2,300 m.
Rhizomatous perennial about 40–70 cm tall, with erect branching stems.
Alternate simple ovate leaves, glandular and often hairy.
Pale tubular flower with flared, reflexed lobes.
Narrow oblong berry 15–30 mm long, with about 10–25 seeds.
Mesa Verde fishhook cactus
Sclerocactus mesae-verdae
Mesa Verde cactus
A rare small cactus of gypsum badlands on the Colorado Plateau. Its depressed stem with 13–17 ribs and hooked central spines is diagnostic; cream to pinkish flowers emerge near the top.
Southwestern Colorado and northwestern New Mexico; arid gypsum soils.
Solitary depressed-globose to ovoid cactus, only a few centimetres tall.
No leaves; tuberculate ribs with straw-colored radial spines and a hooked central spine.
Cream-white to pinkish flower near the stem apex.
Fleshy green to tan fruit, generally indehiscent.
Magellan sphagnum
Sphagnum magellanicum
Magellan peat moss

A peat moss forming red to burgundy cushions. The name was once applied to a much broader complex; in its current strict sense, S. magellanicum is restricted to southern Chile and Argentina. Fine identification in the complex can require microscopic and molecular characters.
Bogs of southern Chile and Argentina, especially Tierra del Fuego.
Moss forming dense tufts and cushions, with upright shoots and terminal heads.
Nerveless leaves made of narrow chlorophyll cells among large hyaline cells.
No flowers; sexual organs occur on specialized branches.
Spherical capsule raised above the tuft on a pseudopodium.
Pale-green Gymnocalycium
Gymnocalycium calochlorum
Calochlorum gymnocalycium

A small Argentine cactus with a flattened stem, low ribs divided into chin-like tubercles and short spines. Funnel-shaped flowers can be larger than the body; their color varies from white-pink to pink.
Argentina, in dry rocky habitats.
Solitary low, broad-globose cactus, often blue-green.
No leaves; low ribs with spaced areoles and a few short spines.
Large pale pink to white funnel-shaped flower near the crown.
Fleshy elongated greenish to pink fruit.
Sauer\'s Turbinicarpus
Turbinicarpus saueri
Sauer\'s pincushion cactus

A miniature cactus of northeastern Mexico, often nearly buried in limestone substrate. Its tubercles carry fine, long, sometimes curved radial spines; pale flowers may be pink. Spine characters vary among populations.
Northeastern Mexico, in arid limestone habitats.
Solitary cactus a few centimetres tall, globose and often partly underground.
No leaves; distinct tubercles bear several fine radial spines.
White to pale pink funnel-shaped flower at the crown.
Small smooth capsule that opens at maturity.
Gielsdorf\'s Turbinicarpus
Turbinicarpus gielsdorfianus
Gielsdorf\'s pincushion cactus

A small Mexican cactus with prominent tubercles and flattened radial spines often arranged like a comb. Spine shape and wool at the crown vary; identification from an illustration alone is less certain than from a specimen.
Mexico, arid parts of the central plateau; limestone outcrops.
Compact solitary globose cactus, partly buried.
No leaves; triangular tubercles bear flattened comb-like radial spines.
Small white to pale pink flower at the crown.
Small dry capsule that opens at maturity.
Tacinga funalis
Tacinga funalis
Caatinga Tacinga
A shrubby cactus of the Caatinga with flattened cladodes and tubular flowers adapted to bird pollination. Young leaves are short-lived and areoles bear fine glochids; the fleshy fruit is a berry.
Northeastern Brazil, in the Caatinga.
Branched shrubby cactus, upright to spreading, formed of flattened segments.
Oval to oblong cladodes; small fugacious leaves on young segments and areoles with glochids.
Orange to red tubular nectar flower with projecting stamens.
Fleshy reddish fruit with areoles and seeds embedded in the pulp.
Rock Tacinga
Tacinga saxatilis
rock-outcrop Tacinga

A cactus of seasonally dry vegetation in central Brazil, associated with rocky outcrops. Its flattened cladodes and orange-red tubular flowers resemble other Tacinga, while compact form and rocky habitat aid recognition.
Central and northeastern Brazil; rocky, often limestone, outcrops.
Compact branched succulent subshrub with flattened segments.
Oval flattened cladodes with spaced areoles, glochids and small deciduous leaves on young shoots.
Orange-red flower with narrow tube and projecting stamens.
Fleshy berry containing flattened seeds.
Stout-spined Melocactus
Melocactus pachyacanthus
Bahia stout-spined melon cactus

A solitary cactus from Bahia, recognizable by its ribbed globose stem and red woolly cephalium at the crown. Tiny pink flowers emerge from the cephalium; elongated red fruits project from it. Ribs bear stout spines.
Eastern Brazil, especially Bahia; dry habitats and limestone outcrops.
Solitary globose blue-green cactus, with a red cephalium appearing in adulthood.
No leaves; deep ribs bear areoles with stout spines.
Tiny pink to magenta flowers inserted in the cephalium.
Elongated red berry projecting from the cephalium, with black seeds.
Nightshade-like Plowmania
Plowmania nyctaginoides
volcano-top Plowmania

A rare high-elevation Mesoamerican shrub famous for exceptionally long tubular flowers, orange with scarlet lobes and a golden throat. Few observations are available, so its range and variation remain poorly known.
Volcanic summits of Chiapas and Guatemala.
Woody branching shrub, usually 1–3 m tall in available descriptions.
Alternate simple oval to elliptic leaves with entire margins.
Long orange tubular corolla with scarlet lobes and yellow throat, often near branch tips.
Dark spherical berry after flowering.
Lance-leaved halothamnus
Halothamnus lancifolius
lance-leaved saltwort
A glabrous, glaucous subshrub of Middle Eastern deserts. Its fleshy broad-based leaves and papery winged fruit distinguish it from H. glaucus, whose leaves are narrower and nearly cylindrical.
Eastern Mediterranean to southern Iran and the Arabian Peninsula; deserts, 0–500 m.
Glabrous glaucous subshrub, branching mostly above, up to about 60 cm.
Alternate succulent triangular-lanceolate leaves with a widened, slightly decurrent base.
Minute flowers among bracts longer than the perianth.
Fruit surrounded by five membranous wings, about 10–15 mm across.
Türckheim\'s Guamatela
Guamatela tuerckheimii
Guamatela
A prostrate Central American subshrub, the sole species in Guamatelaceae. Opposite toothed leaves with palmate venation and pale felted undersides contrast with small flowers and dry follicles.
Southern Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras; humid tropical forests.
Evergreen subshrub, low and spreading over the ground.
Opposite simple toothed leaves with palmate venation and a densely whitish underside.
Small flowers with five floral parts and ten stamens.
Fruit of dehiscent follicles containing several seeds.
Small-flowered Ruizia
Ruizia parviflora
formerly Trochetia parviflora

A rare shrub of Mauritius, now accepted as Ruizia parviflora; Trochetia parviflora is a synonym. Its oblong leaves with rounded bases and small clusters of three white to pinkish flowers are distinctive.
Endemic to Mauritius, currently known from Mount Corps de Garde.
Much-branched low to medium shrub, reaching about 3 m.
Oblong, entire firm leaves with rounded bases; underside finely covered in brown scales.
Small flowers in groups of three; petals no longer than sepals.
Globose capsule; fruits may be grouped in threes.
Affined thyme-moss
Plagiomnium affine
broad-leaved thyme-moss

A moss of moist shaded soils, forming mats with upright stems. Its oval, sharply toothed leaves are broader and more spreading than in several related mosses. Inclined capsules on reddish setae are rare; distinguishing close species can require a dissecting microscope.
Europe and temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere; cool woodland soils and ravines.
Mat-forming moss with stems a few centimetres tall and visible sporophytes.
Oval leaves with a central nerve and sharply toothed margins, spreading from the shoot.
No flowers; sexual organs are borne on leafy stems.
Rare inclined blunt-tipped capsule on a long reddish seta.
